strand: Carbon accounting and UK policy: carbon budgets and pathways (CCC 6CB/7CB, NESO FES 2025), government heat policy and hybrid eligibility (HBS 2021, BUS), appraisal carbon values and electricity emissions factors (DESNZ Green Book supplementary guidance, Oct 2026 data tables), UK ETS prices, GHG conversion factors 2025, marginal vs average emissions in GB, levy rebalancing and Ofgem price cap levels. All sources accessed 2026-11-07.

sources.harvard: Climate Change Committee (2020) The Sixth Carbon Budget: Buildings (sector summary of the Advice, Methodology and Policy reports). London: Climate Change Committee. Available at: https://www.theccc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Sector-summary-Buildings.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: The CCC's Sixth Carbon Budget modelling assumed hybrid heat pumps run in heat pump mode up to 80% of the time, based on Imperial College London work.
claims.quote: Based on work undertaken by Imperial College London our base assumption is that hybrid heat pumps can operate in heat pump mode up to 80% of the time.
claims.locator: Methodology excerpt, 'Hybrid heat pumps' bullet, PDF p. 29 (repeated in Box P3.1, PDF p. 63)

claims.claim: A sensitivity with heat pump mode only 50% of the time made hybrids significantly less cost-effective.
claims.quote: A sensitivity conducted on our scenarios suggests that hybrid heat pumps which only operate in heat pump mode 50% of the time (relative to 80% of the time in the baseline case) are significantly less cost effective.
claims.locator: Policy excerpt, Box on role of hybrid heat pumps, PDF p. 63

claims.claim: Field evidence on hybrid performance was variable and behaviour-dependent.
claims.quote: Trials undertaken by the Energy Systems Catapult have shown that performance can be highly variable and dependent on household heating behaviours.
claims.locator: Methodology excerpt, 'Hybrid heat pumps' bullet, PDF p. 29

claims.claim: The CCC named smart-control standards and gas/electricity price rebalancing as conditions for hybrids to deliver.
claims.quote: In order to overcome challenges of this kind, standards on smart heating controls and operation, and rebalancing of gas and electricity prices, would be important parts of any policy package.
claims.locator: Policy excerpt, Box on role of hybrid heat pumps, PDF p. 63

claims.claim: The CCC presented hybrids as offering public acceptability and near-term deployment benefits.
claims.quote: Unlike a shift straight to an electric heat pump, a switch to hybrid heat pumps would enable people to experience unchanged characteristics of the heating service they receive and avoid disruption
claims.locator: Policy excerpt, Box on role of hybrid heat pumps, PDF p. 62

claims.claim: 6CB technology assumptions: ASHP combined SPF 300% at 40 C flow (2020) and gas boiler efficiency 87%.
claims.quote: Air source heat pumps* 300% ... Gas boiler 87% ... Heat pump efficiencies represent the combined SPF assumed for 2020 at 40°C flow temperature
claims.locator: Methodology excerpt, technology cost and performance table and notes, PDF p. 29 (table rows abridged with ellipses)

claims.claim: The 7CB Balanced Pathway does not model fossil fuel (or hydrogen) hybrid heat pumps; its 'hybrids' are mostly heat pumps paired with point-of-use hot water.
claims.quote: A hybrid heat pump uses a standard heat pump alongside an additional heat source. In our modelling, the most common hybrid is a combination of a heat pump with point-of-use hot water. We do not consider fossil fuel or hydrogen hybrids.

claims.claim: Hybrids (non-fossil) are 6% of heat pumps installed by 2040; ASHP 94%.
claims.quote: These mostly consist of air source heat pumps (94% of the heat pumps installed by 2040), with a smaller role for ground source heat pumps (0.4%) and hybrids (6%).
claims.locator: Section 7.2, Individual heat pumps bullet, printed p. 163 (PDF p. 164)

claims.claim: Heat pump installation trajectory in existing homes.
claims.quote: 60,000 heat pumps were installed in 2023, and this rises to nearly 450,000 in 2030, reaching around 1.5 million by 2035.

claims.claim: Consistent with a 2035 end to sales of new gas boilers.
claims.quote: This aligns with a 2035 phase-out date for ending the sale of new gas boilers.

claims.claim: Hydrogen boilers and hydrogen hybrids are excluded from the Balanced Pathway.
claims.quote: hydrogen boilers and hydrogen heat pump hybrids are not included in the Balanced Pathway.

claims.claim: Balanced Pathway electricity supply intensity: 131 gCO2e/kWh (2023) to 7 (2040) and 1 (2050).
claims.quote: emissions intensity of electricity supply is projected to fall by 95% from 131 gCO2e/kWh in 2023 to 7 gCO2e/kWh by 2040, and by 99% to 1 gCO2e/kWh by 2050

claims.claim: The pathway assumes the electricity:gas price ratio falls from about 4 to 2.2-2.6 by 2040 via levy removal and cost changes.
claims.quote: resulting in the ratio of electricity to gas prices falling from around 4 today to between 2.2 and 2.6 by 2040
claims.locator: Chapter 5/6 summary of Balanced Pathway buildings measures, PDF p. 107

claims.claim: CCC recommends removing levies and policy costs from domestic electricity bills.
claims.quote: Make electricity cheaper by removing levies and other policy costs from domestic electricity bills, to help incentivise consumers to switch to lower-carbon electric options.

claims.claim: Government saw a possible transitional role for hybrids in the 2020s and 2030s but did not rule them in or out for 2050.
claims.quote: we acknowledge that hybrids could play a transitional role in the 2020s and 2030s, but currently remains too early to rule hybrid systems in or out of the 2050 energy mix

claims.claim: Natural gas hybrids are stated to be incompatible with net zero.
claims.quote: natural gas-heat pump hybrids are still reliant on a natural gas supply and therefore are not compatible with Net Zero

claims.claim: HBS defines hybrids and notes controls can optimise on cost or efficiency.
claims.quote: Controls can be used to manage how the different technologies operate together and can be used to optimise on the basis of cost or efficiency.

claims.claim: The carbon reduction from hybrids was evidentially unresolved in 2021.

claims.claim: The LRMEF is a time-weighted annual average for a small, sustained, evenly distributed change in demand.
claims.quote: The change in electricity consumption is assumed to be predictable in advance, so that it is met by generation bought in the wholesale market, and distributed evenly through the day and year

claims.claim: Average factors for footprinting; marginal for sustained changes in appraisal.
claims.quote: Whereas the average emissions factors should be used to account for emissions for the purposes of emissions footprinting, the marginal emissions factor should be used for analysing sustained changes in energy consumption

claims.claim: LRMEF method: DDM to 2026, BID3 Net Zero reference case 2025 from 2027, smoothed power-law curve; 2010 marginal was CCGT at 0.357 kgCO2e/kWh before losses.
claims.quote: From 2027 onwards the DESNZ BID3 Net Zero reference case 2025 has been used. The method adds a small amount of demand to each hour of a year

claims.claim: Table 1 values are conservative for electrification; bespoke analysis needed above ~10-20 TWh/yr.
claims.quote: In most cases the marginal emissions factor in the Data Table will be a conservative estimate of the increased emissions from a policy requiring new electrification

claims.claim: VAT removed from household electricity from 1 Oct 2026 to 31 Mar 2027; gas keeps 5%.
claims.quote: The government has removed VAT from electricity bills from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027.

sources.harvard: Ofgem (2026c) Treatment of ECO and RO in the price cap from April 2026. London: Ofgem, January 2026. Available at: https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-01/Treatment%20of%20ECO%20and%20RO%20in%20the%20price%20cap%20from%20April%202026%20%281%29-20260126113009.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: Budget 2025: Exchequer meets 75% of domestic RO costs 2026/27-2028/29 and ECO/GBIS end on bills; Ofgem applies a straight 75% cut to the RO allowance.
claims.quote: then apply a straight 75% reduction to the resulting RO allowance to reflect government funding for domestic households.

sources.harvard: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (2025b) Energy bill reductions: statement to energy suppliers. London: DESNZ, published 17 December 2025. Available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/energy-bill-reductions-statement-to-energy-suppliers/energy-bill-reductions-statement-to-energy-suppliers (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: From April 2026, 75% of domestic RO costs met by the Exchequer for three years and ECO no longer levied on bills.
claims.quote: From April 2026/27–28/29, 75% of domestic costs associated with the Renewables Obligation ( RO ) will be met by the Exchequer. From April 2026, the Energy Company Obligation ( ECO ) will no longer be levied on energy bills.

sources.harvard: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (2026f) Breathing space on your energy bill. London: DESNZ, published 26 August 2026. Available at: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/breathing-space-on-your-energy-bill (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: VAT removed from household electricity from 1 October 2026, average saving £45/yr, funded for 2026-27.
claims.quote: From 1 October 2026, VAT will be removed from household electricity bills, saving households an average of £45 per year.

sources.harvard: Shepheard, M., Kavan, M., Lucas, E. and Lewis, D. (2024) Cheaper electricity, fairer bills. London: Nesta, 4 December 2024. Available at: https://www.nesta.org.uk/report/cheaper-electricity-fairer-bills/ (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: Policy costs were 16% of a typical electricity bill but 5.5% of a gas bill (Oct-Dec 2024 cap).
claims.quote: Policy costs account for 16% of a typical electricity bill, but only 5.5% of a typical gas bill.

claims.claim: Price ratio 3.9; ASHP running-cost break-even ratio 4.1; removing all levies from electricity gives 3.1; full rebalancing 2.4.
claims.quote: Electricity is currently 3.9 times more expensive than gas. 4.1 is the threshold price ratio where the typical home starts to have lower fuel expenditure with an air-source heat pump than with a gas boiler.
claims.locator: Section 'Rebalancing could dramatically reduce the ratio'

claims.claim: Moving only the RO and FiT levies onto gas achieves most of the rebalancing effect.
claims.quote: Moving only the two main environmental levies – the Renewables Obligation (RO) and the Feed-in-Tariff (FiT) levy – from electricity onto gas would be enough to achieve most of the effects of rebalancing.
claims.locator: Section 'Moving only the largest environmental levies'

sources.harvard: Russon, J. and Wakelin, H. (2026) Rebalancing Electricity Levies in the UK: Impacts on Electricity Bills, Fuel Poverty, and the Clean Heat Transition. Liverpool: The MCS Foundation, March 2026. Available at: https://mcsfoundation.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/MCSF-Rebalancing-Electricity-Levies-in-the-UK-Report-Final.pdf (Accessed: 7 November 2026).

claims.claim: The post-Budget 2025 measures only partly correct the levy imbalance.
claims.quote: These results indicate that the post-Budget interventions go some way towards correcting the imbalance created by the concentration of policy costs on electricity bills, though they do not fully resolve it.
claims.locator: Section on impacts on electrically heated households, PDF p. 36

claims.claim: Just over 60,000 MCS-certified heat pumps were installed in 2025.
claims.quote: In 2025, just over 60,000 MCS-certiﬁed heat pumps were installed.
